title: Encryption & Cryptography
subtitle: Symmetric vs asymmetric, DES/AES facts, hashing, digital signatures & the TLS hybrid handshake

readingSections.title: Cryptography: The Landscape
readingSections.quickSummary: Encryption = reversible (with key); hashing = one-way integrity. Two families: symmetric (one key) and asymmetric (key pair).
content: Cryptography serves four goals: confidentiality (secrecy via encryption), integrity (tamper-evidence via hashing), authentication (identity via certificates/signatures) and non-repudiation (undeniable sending via digital signatures).

Encryption is REVERSIBLE: plaintext + key -> ciphertext, and the right key returns the plaintext. Hashing (MD5, SHA family) is ONE-WAY: a fixed-length fingerprint with no decrypt step - change one bit and the hash changes completely.

Two encryption families exist. Symmetric: ONE shared key both encrypts and decrypts - fast, but the key must reach the other side safely. Asymmetric: a PUBLIC key encrypts, a PRIVATE key decrypts - slow, but the public half can be published freely.

subsections.title: The named algorithms
subsections.content:
Symmetric: DES (56-bit key, 16 rounds, block cipher, bit-oriented), 3DES (DES x3, deprecated), AES (128/192/256-bit keys, 10/12/14 rounds), IDEA, Blowfish, RC4 (stream, broken).
Asymmetric: RSA (factoring), Diffie-Hellman (key exchange), ECC (elliptic curves - small keys, strong).
Hashes: MD5 (broken for security), SHA-1 (deprecated), SHA-2/SHA-3 (current).

quickRevision: Confidentiality from encryption; integrity from hashes; signatures = hash + private key.
tricks: 'Cannot be decrypted' in the stem -> hashing, not encryption.
Speed ranking: symmetric >> asymmetric - that is why TLS uses asymmetric ONLY to exchange a symmetric session key.
MD5/SHA-1 in an option about 'secure today' -> wrong; they are broken/deprecated.
patterns: 'Which algorithm is asymmetric?' -> RSA (only non-symmetric option typically).

pyqPatterns.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
pyqPatterns.question: DES is an example of which option?
pyqPatterns.approach: Bit-oriented cipher - DES encrypts 64-bit blocks with a 56-bit key over 16 rounds.

readingSections.companyNote: One algorithm-classification question (symmetric vs asymmetric vs hash) appears in most security buckets.

readingSections.title: Symmetric vs Asymmetric
readingSections.quickSummary: Symmetric: same key both ways - fast, distribution problem. Asymmetric: public encrypts, private decrypts - solves distribution, computationally heavy.
content: Symmetric cryptography (DES, 3DES, AES, IDEA, Blowfish) uses one secret key for both directions. Strengths: speed - hundreds of times faster than asymmetric. Weakness: KEY DISTRIBUTION - both parties need the same secret, and any insecure channel compromises it; also key scaling (n parties need n(n-1)/2 keys).

Asymmetric cryptography (RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECC) uses mathematically linked key pairs. Publish the public key to the world; keep the private key secret. Anyone can encrypt TO you with your public key; only your private key decrypts. It also enables DIGITAL SIGNATURES: sign with the private key, verify with the public one.
Real systems hybridise: TLS uses asymmetric crypto to authenticate and exchange a fresh symmetric SESSION KEY, then encrypts the bulk traffic symmetrically - fast AND distribution-safe.

subsections.title: Key-scaling maths
subsections.content:
Symmetric keys for n parties: n(n-1)/2 (10 people -> 45 keys).
Asymmetric: n key pairs (10 people -> 10 pairs, 10 public keys published).

quickRevision: Asymmetric: pair, slow, solves distribution + signatures (RSA/ECC/DH).
Hybrid TLS: asymmetric handshake -> symmetric session.
tricks: 'Public key encrypts, private decrypts' - never reversed for confidentiality (reversing = signature).
Key-count questions: symmetric n(n-1)/2 vs asymmetric n.
patterns: 'Which is used for bulk data in TLS?' -> symmetric session cipher.
readingSections.companyNote: The hybrid-TLS story (asymmetric handshake, symmetric bulk) is the exam's favourite crypto narrative.

readingSections.title: DES & AES: The Block-Cipher Facts
readingSections.quickSummary: DES: 64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds, bit-oriented. AES: 128-bit block, 128/192/256-bit keys, 10/12/14 rounds. Rounds = key bits / 32.
content: DES (Data Encryption Standard, 1977): a symmetric BLOCK cipher - encrypts 64-bit blocks with a 56-bit effective key through 16 Feistel rounds. It is a BIT-ORIENTED cipher (the published AXIS PYQ answer). Its 56-bit key is brute-forceable today, so 3DES (triple-DES) extended life before AES replaced it.

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard, 2001, Rijndael): symmetric block cipher with a fixed 128-bit block and three key sizes. The round count follows the key: AES-128 -> 10 rounds, AES-192 -> 12, AES-256 -> 14. Each round runs SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey - the final round skips MixColumns.

Stream vs block: block ciphers encrypt fixed chunks (DES/AES); stream ciphers encrypt bit-by-bit with a keystream (RC4 - now broken). Feistel networks (DES) split halves; AES's Substitution-Permutation network does not.

subsections.title: The one numeric fact (published PYQ)
subsections.content:
'How many processes/rounds turn plaintext into encrypted data in AES-128?' -> 10.
Pattern: rounds = key bits / 32 (128/32 = 10, 192/32 = 12... well, 6; the standard fixes 12; 256/32 = 8... the standard fixes 14). Memorise the trio 10-12-14 directly.

tricks: 16 rounds belongs to DES; 10/12/14 belong to AES - options always cross-list them.
AES-256 -> 14 rounds; AES-192 -> 12; AES-128 -> 10. Climb with the key.
patterns: 'Which is a symmetric block cipher?' - AES/DES (not RSA).

readingSections.title: Hashing & Digital Signatures
readingSections.quickSummary: Hashes fingerprint data one-way (MD5/SHA); digital signatures = hash of the message encrypted with the signer's PRIVATE key.
content: A cryptographic hash (MD5 128-bit, SHA-1 160-bit, SHA-256 256-bit) maps any input to a fixed-length fingerprint: deterministic, one-way (no inverse), avalanche-prone (tiny change = totally different hash), collision-resistant (practically impossible to find two inputs with one hash). Uses: integrity checks, password storage (salted), digital signatures, blockchains.

A DIGITAL SIGNATURE works backwards from encryption: the sender HASHES the message, then encrypts that hash with their PRIVATE key. Anyone verifies by decrypting with the sender's PUBLIC key and comparing hashes - proving origin (authentication) and non-repudiation, since only the private key holder could have signed.
Password storage best practice: store salted hashes, never plaintext or plain encryption - database theft then leaks nothing reversible.

subsections.title: Hash properties checklist
subsections.content:
Deterministic - same input, same output.
One-way - cannot recover input.
Avalanche - one bit flips everything.
Collision-resistant - two inputs, same hash: practically impossible (MD5/SHA-1 fail this today).

quickRevision: Hash = one-way fingerprint: MD5 (broken), SHA-1 (deprecated), SHA-2/3 (current).
Signature = hash encrypted with signer's PRIVATE key; verified with PUBLIC key.
tricks: Signature key direction is OPPOSITE to confidentiality: sign with private, encrypt-to-me with public.
'Cannot be reversed' -> hash. 'Two keys mathematically linked' -> asymmetric.
MD5 in a 'secure today' option -> wrong (collisions demonstrated).
patterns: 'Which ensures a message was not altered?' - hash/digest comparison.
'Which proves the sender cannot deny sending?' - digital signature (non-repudiation).
readingSections.companyNote: Signature-vs-encryption key direction trips many candidates - one deliberate revision kills the trap.

readingSections.title: SSL/TLS & the Hybrid Handshake
readingSections.quickSummary: TLS = modern SSL: certificates authenticate, asymmetric crypto exchanges a symmetric session key, bulk data rides symmetric.
content: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) evolved into TLS (Transport Layer Security) - 'SSL' survives as the colloquial name. TLS provides the padlock on HTTPS: server authentication via CA-signed certificates, key exchange, and encrypted application data.

The hybrid handshake: (1) hello - versions and cipher suites negotiated; (2) server presents its CERTIFICATE; browser verifies the chain to a trusted Certificate Authority; (3) key exchange (RSA or Diffie-Hellman variants) establishes a fresh SYMMETRIC session key; (4) all further traffic encrypts with that fast symmetric cipher (typically AES).
A published AXIS PYQ detail: in SSLv3, padding bits are CONCATENATED with the secret key during MAC computation - textbook (Forouzan) phrasing that appeared verbatim in the exam.

subsections.title: Handshake order
subsections.content:
ClientHello -> ServerHello + Certificate -> key exchange -> session keys derived -> encrypted application data.
TLS 1.3 simplifies to ONE round trip and drops legacy algorithms.

quickRevision: TLS = modern SSL. Certificates authenticate servers.
Asymmetric handshake -> symmetric session key -> fast bulk encryption.
SSLv3 padding bits concatenated with the secret key (PYQ fact).
tricks: Handshake story in order: negotiate -> certify -> exchange -> encrypt-symmetric.
SSLv3 padding = CONCATENATED (published PYQ) - not XORed, not ANDed.
patterns: 'Padlock/padlock not shown' - certificate validity/CA trust issue.
'Session key' - the symmetric key created during the handshake.

pyqPatterns.approach: Concatenated - the Forouzan-textbook line the exam quoted.

formulas.title: Symmetric vs Asymmetric Decision Table

formula.text: One shared key (DES/AES) vs public+private pair (RSA/ECC).

explanation: Symmetric: same key both directions; fast bulk encryption; n(n-1)/2 keys for n parties.
Asymmetric: public encrypts / private decrypts; solves distribution; enables signatures.
Hybrid (TLS): asymmetric handshake -> symmetric session key.
Members: symmetric = DES/3DES/AES/IDEA/Blowfish; asymmetric = RSA/DH/ECC.
formulas.memoryTip: One key = quick; two keys = sure.
formulas.commonMistake: Calling AES asymmetric - AES is the symmetric standard.

formulas.title: AES Rounds Rule

formula.text: Rounds climb with key size: 10, 12, 14 on a fixed 128-bit block.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'how many rounds/processes in AES-x' question.
explanation: 128-bit block fixed; key size selects rounds.
Round ops: SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns (skipped in final round), AddRoundKey.
DES comparison: 16 rounds, 56-bit key - do not cross-match.

formulas.title: DES Fact Card

formula.text: Symmetric Feistel block cipher; 3DES applies it three times.

explanation: 64-bit blocks; 56-bit effective key (8 parity bits dropped from 64).
16 Feistel rounds; bit-oriented cipher (published PYQ).
Broken by brute force today -> 3DES -> AES succession.
formulas.commonMistake: 64-bit KEY - 64 is the block; the key is 56.

formulas.title: Hash vs Encryption

formula.text: Hashes verify; encryption hides. No key reverses a hash.

explanation: Hash properties: deterministic, one-way, avalanche, collision-resistant.
MD5/SHA-1 broken for collisions; SHA-2/3 current.
Password storage: salted hashes only.
Signature = hash signed with private key.
formulas.commonMistake: Decrypting a hash - impossible by design.

formulas.title: Digital Signature Key Direction

formula.text: Confidentiality encrypts to the recipient's public key; signatures sign with the sender's private key.

explanation: Hash the message -> encrypt hash with signer's private key -> anyone verifies with public key.
Provides authentication + integrity + non-repudiation (not confidentiality).
Encrypt-to-someone uses THEIR public key.

example.prompt: Prove a message came from you, unaltered.
steps: Receiver verifies with your public key.

formulas.commonMistake: Signing with the public key - anyone could then forge it.

formulas.title: TLS Hybrid Handshake

formula.text: Certificates authenticate; asymmetric exchange creates a symmetric session key; bulk data rides symmetric.

explanation: ClientHello/ServerHello negotiate suites.
Certificate chain verified to a trusted CA.
Key exchange (ECDHE/RSA) -> fresh symmetric session key.
Bulk traffic: AES-GCM etc. SSLv3 padding fact: concatenated with secret key (PYQ).

example.prompt: Why does TLS use BOTH crypto families?
steps: Asymmetric solves distribution/auth; symmetric is fast.

formulas.memoryTip: Asym to meet, sym to talk.
formulas.commonMistake: Saying TLS encrypts everything with RSA - only the key exchange is asymmetric.

s: Only the holder could sign - non-repudiation.
Only Alice's private key opens it.

aes-rounds.q: Operation skipped in the final round:

s: Keystream cipher - prohibited in TLS now.
Precomputed hash lookup - salt kills it.
Anyone can verify - that's the point.
Signature checked against the publisher's public cert.
Sign the digest, bind the content.

signature-direction.q: If a signature verifies, the message:
s: Any alteration breaks the hash match.
Root of trust in the browser/OS store.

signature-direction.q: Which does a signature NOT provide?
s: Content stays readable - pair with encryption for secrecy.

opts: Hello -> Certificate -> Key exchange -> Encrypted data
tls-hybrid.a: Hello -> Certificate -> Key exchange -> Encrypted data

s: One round trip - faster and leaner.

tls-hybrid.q: Which does TLS NOT hide from a network observer?

opts: Asymmetric solves distribution; symmetric is fast
tls-hybrid.a: Asymmetric solves distribution; symmetric is fast

s: Fingerprints detect change; secrecy needs encryption.

crypto-drill.q: Key exchange without sharing secrets upfront:
s: Public derivation of a shared secret.

opts: Hash -> encrypt hash with private key
Encrypt whole message with public key
crypto-drill.a: Hash -> encrypt hash with private key

s: The two parameter sets, never crossed.

opts: Secrecy lives in the key, not the algorithm's secrecy
crypto-drill.a: Secrecy lives in the key, not the algorithm's secrecy

mcqs.q: Symmetric encryption uses:
opts: A public and private key pair
The same key to encrypt and decrypt
exp: One shared secret key both directions - DES/AES family.

mcqs.q: Asymmetric encryption uses:
exp: Public key encrypts; private key decrypts - RSA family.

mcqs.q: Which algorithm is ASYMMETRIC?
exp: RSA = Rivest-Shamir-Adleman key-pair cryptography.
AES/DES/IDEA are symmetric.

mcqs.q: AES-128 performs how many rounds?
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: 16 is DES's count.

mcqs.q: AES-256 performs how many rounds?
exp: Largest key, most rounds: 14.

mcqs.q: DES has an effective key length of:
exp: 56 effective bits (64-bit blocks; 8 parity bits dropped).

mcqs.q: DES runs for how many rounds?
exp: 16 Feistel rounds - the number that gets swapped into AES options.

mcqs.q: DES is classified as a:
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Published PYQ: DES is a bit-oriented (block) cipher.

mcqs.q: A hash function is:
exp: Fingerprints verify integrity; there is no decrypt step.

mcqs.q: Which is a HASH algorithm?
exp: SHA = Secure Hash Algorithm family.
AES/DES encrypt; RSA uses key pairs.

mcqs.q: A digital signature is created with the sender's:
exp: Sign with the PRIVATE key; anyone verifies with the public one.

mcqs.q: A digital signature provides:
exp: It proves who sent it and that it is unaltered - it does NOT hide content.

mcqs.q: TLS (HTTPS) encrypts bulk traffic with:
exp: Hybrid model: asymmetric handshake creates a symmetric session key for speed.

mcqs.q: The server's identity in HTTPS is proven by:
exp: The certificate chain anchors to a trusted Certificate Authority.

mcqs.q: In SSLv3, padding bits are ______ with the secret key.
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Textbook (Forouzan) line the exam quoted: padding bits are concatenated with the secret key.

mcqs.q: AES operates on blocks of:
exp: Block is fixed at 128 bits; only the KEY varies (128/192/256).
64-bit blocks belong to DES.

mcqs.q: Which AES round operation is SKIPPED in the final round?
exp: Final round omits MixColumns.

mcqs.q: The main weakness of symmetric cryptography is:
exp: Both parties need the same secret - delivery is the hard part; asymmetric solves it.

mcqs.q: For n people to ALL communicate privately with symmetric keys, how many keys are needed?
exp: Every pair needs its own key: n choose 2 = n(n-1)/2 - 10 people = 45 keys.

mcqs.q: Which hash is considered BROKEN for security purposes?
exp: MD5 collisions are practical; SHA-1 deprecated; SHA-2/3 current.

mcqs.q: Password storage best practice:
opts: Reversible encryption with a shared key
exp: Salted hashes defeat rainbow tables and leak nothing reversible.

mcqs.q: RSA's security rests on:
exp: Factoring the product of two large primes is the hard problem.

mcqs.q: ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) offers:
exp: Smaller keys, same strength - ideal for constrained devices.

mcqs.q: 3DES means:
exp: Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt with two or three DES keys - deprecated now.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the TLS handshake is TRUE?
opts: Asymmetric crypto exchanges a symmetric session key
Symmetric crypto exchanges an RSA key
exp: Certificates authenticate; key exchange creates the session key; symmetric does the bulk work.

mcqs.q: Encrypting a message with the RECIPIENT's public key provides:
exp: Only their private key can open it - confidentiality to them.

mcqs.q: Signing with your private key lets ANYONE:
exp: Public-key verification proves origin and integrity - not secrecy.

mcqs.q: A 'salt' in password hashing is:
exp: Salts make identical passwords hash differently - rainbow tables die.

mcqs.q: Which is a STREAM cipher?
exp: RC4 encrypts bit-by-bit with a keystream (now broken); AES/DES are block ciphers.

mcqs.q: Diffie-Hellman is used for:
opts: Key exchange over an insecure channel
exp: Two parties derive a shared secret publicly without transmitting it.

mcqs.q: Avalanche effect means:
opts: One input bit change alters the whole output hash
exp: Tiny change -> completely different digest - tamper evidence.

mcqs.q: Which key does a receiver use to decrypt a message encrypted for them?
exp: Encrypt-to-me uses my public key; only MY private key opens it.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE about AES block size?
opts: Fixed 128 bits regardless of key size
exp: Key size varies the rounds; the block stays 128.

mcqs.q: Non-repudiation means the sender:
exp: Only the private key holder could have signed - denial is impossible.

mcqs.q: Which is the CURRENT recommended hash family?
exp: MD5 broken, SHA-1 deprecated, SHA-2/3 stand.

mcqs.q: A Certificate Authority's role is to:
opts: Sign/verify certificates binding keys to identities
exp: The CA vouches that a public key belongs to a named entity.

mcqs.q: Which cipher would protect a satellite link with minimal CPU?
exp: ECC delivers strength with tiny keys - ideal for constrained hardware.

mcqs.q: TLS 1.3 improved on 1.2 by:
opts: One-round-trip handshake and dropping legacy algorithms
exp: Faster, leaner, legacy-cipher-free.

mcqs.q: Which is a BLOCK cipher mode concept?
exp: Modes (CBC/GCM/CTR) need unique IVs/nonces - reuse breaks security.

mcqs.q: Kerckhoffs's principle states security must rely on:
opts: The key being secret, not the algorithm
exp: Assume the enemy knows the system; the key carries all secrecy.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE about 3DES today?
opts: Deprecated - effectively 112-bit security, being phased out
exp: AES replaced it; 3DES lingers in legacy banking systems.

mcqs.q: Perfect forward secrecy means:
opts: Compromised long-term keys don't reveal past session keys
exp: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE) gives each session independent keys.

mcqs.q: A collision in hashing means:
opts: Two inputs produce the same hash
exp: Collisions break integrity guarantees - why MD5/SHA-1 fell.

mcqs.q: Which encryption protects data AT REST on a lost laptop?
exp: BitLocker/FileVault encrypt stored data; TLS protects transit only.

mcqs.q: Which statement about key length is TRUE?
opts: Asymmetric keys are always shorter for equal strength
exp: Asymmetric needs far longer keys for equivalent strength - ECC closes the gap.

mcqs.q: The 'session key' in TLS lives:
opts: Only for that connection, then discarded
exp: Fresh per-session keys limit blast radius - forward secrecy extends this.

mcqs.q: Which algorithm would sign a software update so users verify the publisher?
exp: Code-signing certificates + private-key signatures - verified against the public key.

mcqs.q: Encryption + hash + signature together give:
exp: The full security stack - each tool covers one goal.

mcqs.q: A published AXIS PYQ asks how many 'processes' convert plaintext to ciphertext in AES-128. The answer 10 refers to:
opts: The 10 rounds of the AES-128 schedule
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Each round applies the four operations; 10 rounds total for the 128-bit key.

mcqs.q: Why does the final AES round skip MixColumns?
opts: It would be redundant - no security gain before the last key addition
exp: A final MixColumns adds nothing invertible to cryptanalysis - the standard omits it.

mcqs.q: An attacker has n users' symmetric network. Adding an (n+1)th user requires how many NEW keys?
exp: The new member shares a key with EACH existing member: n new keys - the scaling problem asymmetric crypto solves.

mcqs.q: Which attack does a per-message unique nonce/IV specifically prevent?
exp: IV/nonce reuse in modes like CTR/GCM leaks keystream - uniqueness is mandatory.

mcqs.q: Published AXIS trivia: SSLv3 MAC padding bits are concatenated with the secret key. This construction appears in:
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: A textbook detail quoted verbatim - memorise 'concatenated' for this exact question.

mcqs.q: Why do signatures hash the message FIRST?
opts: Signing a fixed-size digest is efficient and binds the signature to exact content
exp: Hash-then-sign: efficiency + integrity binding; signing raw long messages would be impractical.

mcqs.q: Which scenario breaks forward secrecy?
opts: Server's long-term RSA key stolen, enabling decryption of recorded old handshakes (no ECDHE)
exp: Without ephemeral key exchange, stealing the static key unlocks ALL recorded sessions - ECDHE prevents this.

mcqs.q: Match: DES-? ; AES-? ; RSA-? ; SHA-?
opts: 56-bit key; 10/12/14 rounds; key pairs; one-way digest
exp: DES 56-bit/16 rounds; AES 10/12/14; RSA key pairs; SHA one-way digests - option A alone aligns all four.

mcqs.q: A CA's root certificate is compromised. Blast radius:
opts: Every certificate chaining to that CA becomes forgeable
exp: The root anchors the whole chain - revocation and re-issuance at scale follow.

mcqs.q: Which correctly orders the TLS 1.2 handshake?
opts: Hello -> Certificate -> Key exchange -> Finished (symmetric from here)
exp: Negotiate, authenticate, exchange, then encrypted Finished under the new session keys.

mcqs.q: Why hash passwords with a salt instead of encrypting them?
opts: Hashes can't be reversed; salts defeat precomputed tables - a DB leak reveals nothing usable
exp: Verification only needs hash equality - reversible storage is an unnecessary risk.

mcqs.q: Order by historical succession:
exp: 1977 DES, late-90s 3DES stopgap, 2001 AES standardisation.
